\chapter{Xihuan — What You Like}
\label{ch:zh-xihuan}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I like and do not like, and ask somebody else what they like.}

Eighteen strokes and one verb, and the liking frame every other language in this series makes a beginner turn round: in Mandarin the liker is simply the subject.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[xǐ]{\zh{喜} — twelve strokes, stacked in four bands}

\label{lesson:ZH-W28-xi}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and its first character is the tallest in the book.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shíbā suì — nǐ hé wǒ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǒu} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎokàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{míngzi} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — read it downwards, in four bands}
\begin{quote}
\zh{喜}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Twelve strokes} — more than any character you have written. Do not count them. \textbf{Read the character downwards in four bands}, and every band is a shape you already know.

\textbf{Band one — \zh{士}, three strokes.} A long \textbf{héng} across the top, a \textbf{shù} down through it, a shorter \textbf{héng} beneath. That is \zh{十} with a longer bar on top.

\textbf{Band two — \zh{口}, three strokes.} Left side, joined top-and-right, closing floor. The same mouth as always.

\textbf{Band three — two short strokes}, a small pair leaning apart under the \zh{口}.

\textbf{Band four — one long héng, then \zh{口} again.} Stroke 9 is the widest stroke in the character, running edge to edge, and it carries everything above it. Then the lower \zh{口}, in its usual three.

3 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 = twelve.

\textbf{Top before bottom, all the way down.} Two \zh{口}, and both of them are written the way you have written \zh{口} since \zh{吗}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{士} — \zh{口} — the small pair — the long bar — \zh{口}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{喜}, all twelve, downwards
  \item \emph{Cover:} write it again and count the bands, not the strokes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{喜} have? (\textbf{Twelve}.) How many bands? (\textbf{Four}.) How many of them are \zh{口}? (\textbf{Two} — the middle band and the last.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E5\%96\%9C.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{喜}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[huān]{\zh{欢} — six strokes, and two of them are already yours}

\label{lesson:ZH-W28-huan}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and this one is short by comparison.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{xǐ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yǒu} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hǎokàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{zì} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — \zh{又} again, then \zh{欠}}
\begin{quote}
\zh{欢}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes}, and the first two are ones you wrote one chapter ago.

The left half is \textbf{\zh{又}}, the hand:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{héngpiě} — a short flat start that turns and falls to the lower left
  \item the \textbf{nà}, crossing it and falling to the lower right
\end{enumerate}

That is exactly how \zh{对} begins. Same pair, same order, same place in the square.

The right half is \zh{欠} \emph{qiàn}, a person with an open mouth:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item a short \textbf{piě} at the top, falling left
  \item the \textbf{hénggōu} — a horizontal that hooks down at its end
  \item the long \textbf{piě}, falling from under the hook to the lower left
  \item the \textbf{nà}, falling to the lower right and reaching furthest of all
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Strokes 5 and 6 are the character's legs}, and they must both reach out. Cramped, \zh{欢} looks like something else; spread, it is unmistakable.

After \zh{喜}'s twelve, six will feel like nothing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{又} — the two strokes that also open \zh{对}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{欢}, all six
  \item \emph{Cover:} write \zh{对} and \zh{欢} side by side and check the left halves match
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes does \zh{欢} have? (\textbf{Six}.) Which character shares its left half? (\textbf{\zh{对}}.) Which two strokes are the legs? (\textbf{The fifth and sixth} — both must reach out.)

Source: \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/\%E6\%AC\%A2.json}{Hanzi Writer Data \zh{欢}, pinned stroke paths and medians}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[xǐhuan]{\zh{喜欢} — what you like}

\label{lesson:ZH-C28-xihuan}



\begin{quote}
Two characters in, and now they say something.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{huān} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hé} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gè} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kàn — kànjiàn — hǎokàn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{míng} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{喜欢}} is \emph{xǐhuan} — \textbf{third tone, then nothing.}

\zh{喜} is third tone, the dip. \zh{欢} is first tone on its own — but inside this word it \textbf{loses its tone altogether} and goes light: \emph{xǐ-huan}, not \emph{xǐ-huān}. That is the same thing \zh{早上} does to \zh{上}, and \zh{名字} to \zh{字}.

Say it once slowly and once at speed: \textbf{xǐ huan}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the liker is the subject, and that is all}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{person + \zh{喜欢} + the thing liked.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我喜欢看书}} \emph{wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū} — I like reading. \textbf{\zh{我喜欢中国}} — I like China. \textbf{\zh{你喜欢汉语吗}} — do you like Chinese?
\end{quote}

That is an ordinary sentence with an ordinary verb and an ordinary object, and saying so is the point. Spanish and Italian make a beginner turn the sentence round: Spanish says \emph{me gusta el libro} — \textquotedblleft{}the book pleases me\textquotedblright{} — and Italian says \emph{mi piace}, with the liker in an object slot and the thing liked as the subject. Learners spend weeks on it.

\textbf{Mandarin asks nothing of you here.} The person who likes goes in front, the verb does not change, and the thing liked follows. It is the same shape as \zh{我看书}.

And \zh{不} works on it normally, which \zh{有} did not:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我不喜欢看书}} — I don't like reading.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{xǐhuan} — \zh{喜欢}, and let \zh{欢} go light
  \item \zh{我喜欢看书}
  \item \zh{我不喜欢看书}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tones does \zh{喜欢} carry? (\textbf{Third, then none} — \zh{欢} goes light.) Who goes in front of it? (\textbf{The person who likes} — no inversion.) Does \zh{不} negate it normally? (\textbf{Yes} — \zh{我不喜欢}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nǐ xǐhuan shénme]{\zh{你喜欢什么} — what do you like?}

\label{lesson:ZH-C28-xihuan-shenme}



\begin{quote}
Four in, and this lesson joins two chapters that never met.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{xǐhuan} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hé} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gè} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shū} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the question, and where \zh{什么} sits}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{你喜欢什么}} \emph{nǐ xǐhuan shénme} — \textbf{what do you like?}
\end{quote}

Four words, and all of them were already in the book except \zh{喜欢}.

\textbf{Now look at where \zh{什么} is.} It is at the END, in exactly the slot the answer would occupy:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\zh{你喜欢什么}} — what do you like? — \textbf{\zh{我喜欢书}} — I like books.
\end{quote}

\textbf{Mandarin does not move a question word.} English hauls \emph{what} to the front and reshuffles everything behind it — \emph{you like what} becomes \emph{what do you like}, with a \emph{do} invented on the way. Mandarin leaves \zh{什么} exactly where the answer goes and changes nothing else. Question and answer have the same shape, word for word.

That is why no \zh{吗} is needed here. \zh{吗} makes a yes-or-no question; a sentence that already contains \zh{什么} is a question, and adding \zh{吗} would be wrong.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{你喜欢汉语吗}} — do you like Chinese? \emph{(yes or no)} \textbf{\zh{你喜欢什么}} — what do you like? \emph{(name it)}
\end{quote}

And the whole exchange, with the particle from the last chapter:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\zh{你喜欢什么}} — \textbf{\zh{我喜欢看书你呢}}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{你喜欢什么}
  \item \zh{我喜欢看书你呢}
  \item \zh{你喜欢汉语吗} — and hear why this one needs \zh{吗}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \zh{什么} stand? (\textbf{Where the answer goes} — at the end.) Does Mandarin move it to the front? (\textbf{No} — nothing moves.) Why is there no \zh{吗}? (\textbf{A sentence with \zh{什么} in it is already a question}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\zh{我喜欢看书}}

\label{lesson:ZH-C28-practice}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter of the tranche closes here.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nǐ xǐhuan shénme} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ shíbā suì — nǐ hé wǒ} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ yǒu yí ge míngzi} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{shū} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{wǒ} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — liking, said plainly}]
Two characters, eighteen strokes, one verb — and with it a whole area of talk this book could not enter:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我喜欢看书}} — I like reading. \textbf{\zh{我不喜欢看书}} — I don't. \textbf{\zh{你喜欢什么}} — what do you like? \textbf{\zh{你喜欢汉语吗}} — do you like Chinese?
\end{quote}

Nothing there is inverted, nothing agrees, nothing moves. The liker is the subject; the thing liked is the object; \zh{什么} stands where the answer stands. Spanish and Italian both make you turn that round; Mandarin does not.

And now the whole tranche can be said in one breath, because every piece of it is yours:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\zh{我是中国人} — \zh{我十八岁} — \zh{我有一个名字} — \zh{我喜欢看书} — \zh{你呢}}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Listen.} \emph{Wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū. Nǐ xǐhuan shénme?}

\textbf{Speak.} Say what you like; ask what the other person likes; hand it back with \zh{你呢}.

\textbf{Read.} \zh{我喜欢看书} — \zh{你喜欢什么}

\textbf{Write.} \zh{喜} — four bands, twelve strokes. \zh{欢} — \zh{又}, then \zh{欠}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{我喜欢看书} \zh{我不喜欢看书}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \zh{你喜欢什么} — \zh{我喜欢书你呢}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{喜} \zh{欢}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I like reading.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\zh{我喜欢看书}}.) Where does \zh{什么} go in the question? (\textbf{At the end, where the answer goes}.) And what does Mandarin ask you to turn round here? (\textbf{Nothing at all}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
